771.title: Gobind is everything
771.hook: sabh gobind hai: everything is Gobind; there is nothing without Him (Asa, Namdev, ang 485)
771.howItsDone: Namdev's hymn with the refrain sabh gobind hai is sung in kirtan as gurbani, and Sikhs draw on it to speak of the One present in every heart and all of creation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dehura: Namdev sang at the back wall, and the temple turned to face him. Your line was low, honest, and received.

Snap the cord of a necklace and you learn something fast. The beads go everywhere: under the couch, into the rug, one rolling off toward the door. While the cord held, you barely noticed it. You were looking at the beads. Namdev, the printer who sang his way into the Guru Granth Sahib, reached for exactly that picture. Where, in the whole world, is the Lord not? His answer, in the original, is short. Everything is Gobind.
screen: `A SNAPPED NECKLACE.` → `THE CORD YOU NEVER NOTICED.` → `WHERE IS THE LORD NOT?`

segments.voice: The hymn is in Raag Asa, on Ang 485, and its refrain is sabh gobind hai, sabh gobind hai, gobind bin nahi koi. In paraphrase: everything is Gobind, everything is Gobind; without Gobind there is nothing at all. Gobind is one of the names for the Lord in the Granth. Namdev gives two pictures. The first is the necklace: as one thread runs through countless beads, so the Lord runs through everything, warp and weft. The second is water. Waves, foam and bubbles are not separate from the water. They rise and fall and look like many things, but they're water all the way through. Then Namdev admits this isn't obvious. In the same hymn he says the world's dazzling pictures keep people bewildered, and only a rare one understands. That's honest. On plenty of days we see beads, not thread, waves, not water. So what does he do? He says the Guru's teaching woke his mind, and he invites the listener: look at the Lord's creation, and think it over in your heart. In every heart, within all, there is only the One. Notice the word think. Namdev isn't asking us to pretend the beads aren't there. The colors, the people, the dishes in the sink all stay. He's asking us to notice the thread through them. Sikhs sing this hymn as gurbani, and its whole teaching fits on one line.

segments.voice: Let your eyes land on one thing nearby, a cup, a window, your own hand, rest there a few breaths, and say inside, sabh gobind hai. Then a second thing, farther away, and a third, a sound, a person or the air itself, letting Namdev's line be the thread through all three. Don't force a feeling; if you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.
Gobind. One of the names for the Lord in the Granth: the thread through every bead, the water in every wave, Namdev's refrain sabh gobind hai.
Your line: everything is gobind. The thread is there even on the days you only see beads. Day seven hundred seventy-one.

772.title: The sultan's demand
772.hook: Namdev sings of a sultan who demanded a miracle, and of the Lord who saved him (Bhairao, Namdev)
772.howItsDone: Namdev's hymn of the sultan is sung as gurbani, and Sikhs often recall it alongside the Gurus' teaching that devotees should not seek to display miraculous powers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gobind: the one thread through the beads and the water in every wave. Your line was everything is gobind.

Prove it. Two words that can corner anyone. Show me your God does something, right here, right now, or else. In one of his hymns, Namdev tells of the day a ruler said exactly that to him. Not a friend teasing, but a sultan, with power behind the words and Namdev's life on the table. The printer who sang that everything is Gobind is suddenly asked to make Gobind perform.
screen: `PROVE IT.` → `A SULTAN, AND A THREAT.` → `MAKE GOBIND PERFORM.`

segments.voice: The hymn is in Raag Bhairao, around Ang 1165. In paraphrase: the sultan says, listen, Namdev, let me see the works of your Lord. He has Namdev bound, and a dead cow is set before him. Bring this cow back to life, says the sultan, or I'll cut off your head right here. Now Namdev's answer, the heart of the day. How can this be? Nothing happens by my doing. Whatever the Lord does, that is what happens. He won't put on a show, or claim a power that isn't his. And he won't drop the Lord to save his neck either. The hymn holds him right there, under threat, honest about what he can and can't do. Then the turn. The hymn says the Lord came to Namdev's side, the cow rose up, and the sultan, shaken, came asking forgiveness. It tells the rescue quickly. It lingers longer on the moment before, when Namdev had nothing to offer but the truth. And look where the hymn puts the credit. Not on Namdev. He refused to be the miracle worker the sultan wanted. He stayed a devotee, and the saving came from beyond him. That's why today's line has two halves. Namdev was saved. He was never shown off.

773.title: Namdev close
773.hook: a low-caste printer whose songs sit inside the Guru's book, named by a Guru as one who found freedom
773.howItsDone: Sikhs sing Namdev's hymns in kirtan as gurbani, and the Gurus' naming of Namdev and Kabir by their trades is often recalled when Sikhs speak about the rejection of caste.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sultan: raise the dead cow or else, and Namdev saying nothing happens by his doing. Your line was saved, not shown.

Namaa chheeba. Namdev the printer. That's how a Sikh Guru names him in a hymn, by his trade, the very thing some people of his day held against him. The Guru doesn't hide it or polish it. He says it plainly, and then says what Namdev found. Five days with this cloth printer: his tools, his cup of milk, the temple at his back, the thread through the beads, the sultan's threat. Today we close his pages by hearing how the Gurus heard him.
screen: `NAMDEV THE PRINTER.` → `NAMED BY HIS TRADE.` → `HOW THE GURUS HEARD HIM.`

segments.voice: The line is in Sri Raag, on Ang 67, in a hymn of Guru Amar Das, the third Guru. In paraphrase: Namdev the printer and Kabir the weaver found liberation through the perfect Guru. They recognized the Word, and their ego and their caste fell away. The sentence starts with two working men, named by work others ranked low, and it ends with freedom. Caste isn't argued with. It just falls away, like a label with nothing left to stick to. Now gather Namdev's week into that line. At his printing table, his mind was the measuring yard and his tongue the scissors, and he asked what caste and lineage had to do with the Name. He set down a cup of milk and pleaded until the Lord drank. Thrown out of a temple, he sang at the back wall, and the temple turned. With a string of beads he showed the One thread through everything. Bound before a sultan, he refused to perform and said nothing happens by his doing. Every scene is low to the ground: a workbench, a cup of milk, the back of a building, a prisoner's place. And in each one, the song ends higher than where it began. Sikhs sing his hymns as gurbani, the Guru's word: a printer whose caste was counted low, and whose songs now sit in the Guru's own book.

774.title: The shoemaker of Benares
774.hook: Ravidas, a leather-worker whose family were counted low, sings that the leading Brahmins now bow to him (Malar, Ravidas, ang 1293)
774.howItsDone: Ravidas's hymns are sung in gurdwaras as gurbani, and Sikhs and Ravidassia communities honor him as a saint whose life challenged caste.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Namaa chheeba: Namdev the printer, named by his trade in a Guru's hymn. Your line was low caste, high song.

Some people learn to hide where they come from. They soften the accent, skip the hometown, let others guess. Ravidas did the opposite. Tradition says he worked leather in Benares, the holy city on the Ganges, at a bench where shoes were cut and stitched and mended. Some people of his day wouldn't touch a leather-worker, or drink from the same cup. Yet his hymns sit inside the Guru Granth Sahib, and in one of them he says, without any shame, exactly where he came from.
screen: `HIDE WHERE YOU COME FROM?` → `A BENCH IN BENARES.` → `HE SAYS WHERE HE CAME FROM.`

segments.voice: The hymn is in Raag Malar, on Ang 1293. Its turn, in paraphrase: my people work in leather, and every day they carry dead cattle around Benares. Now the leading Brahmins bow down before me, for I, Ravidas your servant, have taken shelter in your Name. Hear the order of those lines. He starts with the hardest thing to say. Not a soft word for his trade, but the work itself: hauling dead cattle through the lanes of a holy city. Then the reversal. The very people at the top of that world now bow to him. And notice what he credits. Not his talent, not his luck. The Name. He has taken shelter there, and that shelter changed how he is seen. The second turn: Ravidas doesn't try to escape his family. He names them first, before he names himself, and keeps them in the song, dead cattle and all. The third turn is the Sikh book. The Granth keeps Ravidas's hymns inside the ragas, under his own name. In gurdwaras his words are sung as gurbani, and Sikhs bow to the book that holds them. A leather-worker's song stands in the same place as a Guru's. He didn't trade his family's name for a grander one. He sang with it.

775.title: Begampura, the city without sorrow
775.hook: Ravidas sings of a city without sorrow, tax or fear, where all walk free (Gauri, Ravidas, ang 345)
775.howItsDone: Ravidas's Begampura hymn is sung in gurdwaras as gurbani, and Sikhs and Ravidassia communities often recall it when speaking of a world without caste or fear.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ravidas, whose people carried dead cattle, singing that the Brahmins now bowed to him. Your line was the shoemaker's song.

What would a city look like if nobody in it were afraid? No one dreading the tax collector. No one shut out of a street because of their family. No one first-class and no one second. A leather-worker in Benares, from a family some people kept at the edges, sang about exactly that city, and he gave it a name. It's in the Guru Granth Sahib: Begampura.
screen: `A CITY WHERE NO ONE IS AFRAID?` → `A LEATHER-WORKER NAMES IT.` → `THROUGH THE GATE.`

segments.voice: The hymn is in Raag Gauri, on Ang 345. In paraphrase, Ravidas sings: Begampura is the name of the city. There's no sorrow there and no anxiety. No tax, no tribute, no property to worry over. No fear, no wrongdoing, no dread of decline. I've found a home of my own now, brother, where all is well. The hymn explains its own name: the place where sorrow doesn't live. Now look at what's missing. Tax and tribute, the things a powerful man could squeeze out of a poor one. Fear. Ranking. These are weights that press on the poor, and Ravidas builds his city by taking them off, one at a time. Then, in paraphrase: the rule there is steady and lasting; there's no second or third, all are one. The people wander freely as they please, and no one stops them. Hear that, nobody stops them, against yesterday's picture of a family carrying dead cattle through the lanes. The free walking is the point. At the close Ravidas signs it as one set free, and says, in paraphrase: whoever is a citizen of that city is my friend. Readers hear Begampura in more than one way. Some hear the soul's home with the Lord, beyond sorrow. Others hear a picture of how a town on earth could be, and some carry this hymn into struggles against caste. The hymn holds both. Begampura is a place where no one is second.

If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.
Begampura. The city Ravidas names and describes in Raag Gauri: no sorrow, no tax, no fear, no second or third, and everyone walking free.

776.title: Sandalwood and castor
776.hook: You are sandalwood and I the poor castor plant beside You, made fragrant by Your nearness (Asa, Ravidas, ang 486)
776.howItsDone: Ravidas's sandalwood hymn is sung in kirtan as gurbani, and Sikhs often use its picture to speak of the sangat, the holy company, whose nearness shapes the one who joins it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Begampura: Ravidas's city with no sorrow, no fear, and no second or third. Your line was the city without sorrow.

Sandalwood is prized for its scent, and its fragrance can linger on whatever it touches. The castor plant is a scrappy, weedy shrub that springs up along roadsides and in waste ground. Nobody plants a castor bush for its smell. Ravidas, who sang a whole city without sorrow, turns now to himself, and reaches for these two plants. He sets them side by side in a hymn, and he knows exactly which one he is.
screen: `SANDALWOOD, PRIZED FOR ITS SCENT.` → `CASTOR, A ROADSIDE WEED.` → `RAVIDAS KNOWS WHICH HE IS.`

segments.voice: The hymn is in Raag Asa, on Ang 486. In paraphrase, Ravidas sings to the Lord: You are sandalwood, and I am the poor castor plant, living close beside You. From a lowly tree I've become a lofty one, for Your sweet fragrance has come to dwell in me. Hear how the change happens. The castor doesn't turn into sandalwood, or train or strive its way to a better scent. It grows near, and the fragrance moves across the gap and settles in. Nearness does the work. Ravidas keeps going with more pairs. In paraphrase: You are silk, white and yellow, and I am a poor worm. Then the refrain: Madho, I seek the shelter of the company of Your holy ones; I'm full of faults, and You are generous. The company of the holy ones, in Sikh words sangat, is where the nearness happens. It's not only the Lord far above. It's the people you stand beside. A gathering where the Name is sung can rub off on whoever sits in it. And this is the leather-worker from two days ago, whose people some refused to touch. He doesn't deny that he feels low. He says it plainly. But he doesn't stay there. A low plant beside sandalwood comes away smelling of something else, not by changing what it is, but by where it chose to stand.

segments.voice: Yesterday, chandan: the plain castor plant beside sandalwood, made fragrant just by standing close. Today, Ravidas is lifted higher still.

Over a king's head, in the old courts of India, an attendant held a canopy. Without a word, it said: this one is honored. Now hold that canopy over a leather-worker from Benares, a man whose trade made people step aside in the street. That's the picture Ravidas paints in a hymn in Raag Maru, and he can hardly believe it himself. His question gives today its name.
screen: `A CANOPY FOR THE KING.` → `HELD OVER A LEATHER-WORKER.` → `WHO BUT YOU?`

segments.voice: The hymn sits on Ang 1106 of the Guru Granth Sahib. In paraphrase, it opens: O Beloved, who but You could do such a thing? Then comes a name for God worth learning: gareeb nivaaj, the one who cherishes the poor. My Lord, Ravidas sings, places the canopy over my forehead. The royal sign, on him. He doesn't soften what he was in other people's eyes. His touch, he says, was counted as polluting the world, and on that very person the Lord has poured mercy. Then the line at the hymn's heart: You raise the lowly to the heights, my Gobind, and You fear no one. That last part is quiet but sharp. Lifting someone a whole town has agreed to keep low takes nerve, and Ravidas's Lord doesn't flinch. Then the hymn opens a door. Ravidas names others carried across the same way: Namdev, Kabir, Trilochan, Sadhna and Sain. Namdev, the cloth-printer whose milk was drunk and whose temple turned, filled this past week; Kabir came earlier in this block; Trilochan, Sadhna and Sain are still ahead on this path. Ravidas lines them up like witnesses: it wasn't only me. The hymn closes, in paraphrase: says Ravidas, listen, holy people, the Lord does everything. So the title is a question that isn't really a question. Who but You is what someone says when they've been lifted, and know they didn't lift themselves.
screen: `GAREEB NIVAAJ: WHO CHERISHES THE POOR.` · `THE CANOPY ON A LEATHER-WORKER'S HEAD.` · `THE LOWLY RAISED, AND NO FEAR.` · then, large: `IT WASN'T ONLY ME.`

segments.voice: Let faces come: someone overlooked at work, a relative people talk past, a neighbor nobody greets, a kid at the edge of the room. Stay with one, and picture a small canopy over them: their name said in front of others, their opinion asked first, a thank-you where it can be heard. If you pray, let Waheguru go with each breath out.
Gareeb nivaaj. The one who cherishes the poor: Ravidas's name for the Lord who held a king's canopy over a leather-worker's head.
Your line: raise the lowly to the heights. The week ran from everything is Gobind, to Namdev's sultan, to Ravidas's city without sorrow. Day seven hundred seventy-seven, done.
